passage: Jahnavi, sit. You think your Akash mama was always this calm? When I was twenty, my hostel roommate copied my project and submitted it before me. The professor believed him, not me. For a week I lay awake replaying that meeting, planning how to let the air out of his bike tyres, how to post his old messages to the whole class. One night I wrote everything in a notebook instead, every ugly plan, and locked it in my trunk. Next morning I went to my friend Deepak's room and talked until the tea went cold. He didn't tell me to calm down; he just listened. Then I started running at five every morning and poured the rest into my exams. Beta, the anger was real. I let it out on paper and on the track, not on his tyres. That is why I have nothing from that year to apologise for.

qa.q: What did Akash write in the notebook?
qa.a: He wrote every ugly plan, and then locked the notebook in his trunk.

qa.q: What was Akash feeling during the week he lay awake?
qa.a: He felt hurt and furious that the professor believed his roommate, and the anger kept replaying the meeting and building revenge plans.

qa.q: What turning point did Akash use at this stage, and why did it work?
qa.a: He let the anger out safely by writing the plans privately, talking to Deepak and then running and studying, so the feeling was spent without adding new harm.

qa.q: How might Deepak have experienced the morning Akash came to talk?
qa.a: Deepak probably saw a friend boiling with anger and chose to listen rather than lecture, which let Akash feel heard instead of judged.

grounding: Shows replayed hurt and revenge fantasies being written down privately, shared with a trusted friend and channelled into running and study so no new harm follows.

passage: The power went out again at nine, and Lalit sat in the dark of the one-room flat he shared with his two younger brothers, phone at eight percent. Santosh's forward still sat on the screen: Lalit's private worry about failing maths, sent to the whole class group as a joke. For two days Lalit had replayed it, drafting replies that would humiliate Santosh back, imagining telling Santosh's parents the secret Santosh had once trusted him with. With the battery dying, he tore a page from his rough book and wrote it all out by candlelight, then folded it into his pocket. He texted Meher, his oldest school friend: 'Can I call tomorrow? I'm so angry it scares me.' She rang early and let him talk for twenty minutes. Afterwards he walked to the ground and ran laps until his legs shook, then opened the maths book Santosh had mocked.

qa.q: Where did Lalit write out his anger?
qa.a: On a page torn from his rough book, by candlelight.

qa.q: What does Lalit's message to Meher suggest about how he felt?
qa.a: It suggests he was frightened by how strong his anger had become and wanted help before it turned into something he would regret.

qa.q: Which choices at this stage kept Lalit's anger from causing new harm?
qa.a: Writing it all out on paper, calling Meher, and then running and studying let the anger move through him instead of into a cruel reply or a betrayed secret.

qa.q: What might Meher be experiencing when Lalit calls her?
qa.a: Meher may feel trusted and a little worried for him, and by simply listening she gives him a safe place to let the anger out.

grounding: Illustrates the replay-and-revenge stage handled by a private written note, a talk with a trusted friend and running and study, despite a power cut and a crowded room.

Mridul read the band's message for the fourth time on the auto home: "We're going ahead with a new drummer. Honestly, you were never reliable." Worse, Keshav, the guitarist, had forwarded it to half the college.

That night in the Kothrud flat Mridul lay awake scripting a post that would tell everyone about Keshav's copied assignments. His thumb hovered over the screen. Instead he opened a private notes file and typed every furious line there, spelling mistakes and all, until his hands stopped shaking.

At midnight he called Dilnaz. She listened for twenty minutes without trying to fix anything, then said, "Write it, don't send it."

The next morning Mridul ran three rounds of the university ground before class. The anger was still there, but it had somewhere to go that did not hurt anyone.

qa.q: Where did Mridul type his furious lines instead of posting them?
qa.a: He typed them into a private notes file on his phone.

qa.q: What was Mridul feeling as he lay awake scripting the post about Keshav?
qa.a: He was hurt and furious after being called unreliable in front of half the college, and he wanted Keshav to feel the same public embarrassment.

qa.q: What turning point is available to Mridul at this stage?
qa.a: He can keep the notes file and the morning runs as his outlet, and later decide calmly whether any conversation with Keshav is worth having, instead of acting on a midnight urge.

qa.q: How might Dilnaz see her role that night?
qa.a: Dilnaz probably felt trusted and wanted to steady Mridul without judging, which is why she listened for a long time before giving one short piece of advice.

grounding: It shows a young adult putting revenge urges into a private note, a talk with a trusted friend and exercise so the anger does not cause new harm.

passage:
"He said it in front of the whole team, Jeevan. 'Pradeep drops catches because he's lazy.' Everyone laughed."

"I was there. It was rotten."

"I keep playing it back. Every time I close my eyes I see myself telling the group chat that he paid someone to write his lab reports."

"Did he?"

"I don't even know! That's how angry I am."

Jeevan pushed a notebook across the hostel desk. "Put all of it in here first. The chat, the laughing, what you'd love to say to him. Nobody reads it."

"And then?"

"Then nets. Six o'clock. You bowl at me till your arm hurts."

Pradeep wrote two full pages, pressing so hard the pen tore the paper. At the nets he bowled fast and wild, then slower. Walking back, he said, "I still want to shout at him. I just don't want to lie about him anymore."

qa.q: What did Jeevan push across the hostel desk?
qa.a: Jeevan pushed a notebook across the hostel desk.

qa.q: How can you tell that Pradeep feels consumed by anger and humiliation?
qa.a: He keeps replaying the moment, imagines spreading a rumour he admits may be untrue, and presses so hard he tears the paper, which shows how humiliated and furious he is.

qa.q: What could a friend like Jeevan keep doing after this evening?
qa.a: Jeevan could check in over the next few days and invite Pradeep to the nets again, so the anger keeps a safe outlet while Pradeep decides whether to raise the insult with the captain directly.

qa.q: What would change if Pradeep had posted in the group chat that night?
qa.a: He would have spread a claim he could not back up, hurting the other player and his own name, and turning one bad moment into a bigger conflict.

grounding: The scene shows revenge fantasies being written down privately, shared with a trusted friend and burned off in exercise instead of acted on.

passage:
The screenshot went round the class group on a Tuesday: my message to Yash, the one where I admitted I was scared of failing statistics, with his caption, "Drama queen alert."

For about a week I replayed it everywhere. In the metro I rehearsed the perfect cruel reply. In the shower I imagined sharing the thing Yash had told me about his parents, just to see his face.

What I actually did was smaller. I bought a cheap notebook and wrote down every mean sentence I wanted to send, then closed it. I told Tenzin, my oldest friend, the whole thing over chai, and Tenzin said, "Maria, you're allowed to be this angry. Just don't become the person who screenshots."

Then I used the rage on statistics. Two hours every evening. I passed with a better grade than I had hoped for, and the notebook stayed shut.

qa.q: What was the caption on the screenshot?
qa.a: The caption was "Drama queen alert."

qa.q: What does Maria's imagining of sharing Yash's secret suggest about how Maria felt that week?
qa.a: It suggests Maria felt deeply betrayed and humiliated and wanted Yash to feel the same exposure, even though Maria never acted on it.

qa.q: Which choice worked at this stage, and why?
qa.a: Writing the cruel replies in a notebook and closing it worked, because the anger was expressed fully without reaching Yash or creating a second betrayal.

qa.q: How might Tenzin see what happened?
qa.a: Tenzin likely saw a friend who had been genuinely wronged and wanted to protect Maria from turning that hurt into the same kind of harm.

grounding: A young adult keeps revenge thoughts in a private notebook, confides in a trusted friend and pours the energy into study.

passage:
Athletics coach's note, college ground, Saturday
Chandrika has been furious since her relay partner told the selectors she'd "slacked" in practice, which cost her the state trip. On Monday she told me she'd thought of posting the partner's old message screenshots online. She didn't.
What I've seen since: every evening she runs four extra laps, hard, then sits on the bench writing in a small notebook she keeps in her bag. She told me it's where she writes the things she'd like to shout. On Wednesday I saw her talking for a long time with Kishore from the hockey team, who mostly nodded. Yesterday she laughed at practice for the first time in two weeks. Her times have also improved.
What I did next: I told her that her anger made complete sense, and that I was glad she was letting it out on the track and in the notebook rather than online. I've put her name forward for the next trials.

qa.q: How many extra laps does Chandrika run each evening?
qa.a: She runs four extra laps, hard, every evening.

qa.q: What was Chandrika feeling after her partner's words to the selectors?
qa.a: Chandrika felt furious and hurt, angry enough to think of posting the partner's old messages online.

qa.q: Which of Chandrika's choices helped, and why?
qa.a: Writing in a private notebook, talking to Kishore and running hard let her feel the anger safely, so it didn't become a post that would cause new harm.

qa.q: How might Kishore experience these long talks?
qa.a: Kishore may feel trusted and glad to help simply by listening, even without giving advice.

grounding: Shows a young adult letting anger be felt safely through private writing, a trusted friend and hard exercise instead of acting on revenge.
